idiom_name: self-describing event envelope (stable type id + occurrence timestamp + payload) published on a channel; consumers decode by type
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define each event as an immutable payload type carrying the facts of the occurrence (who, what, when), give it a stable type identifier that never changes meaning, and wrap it in the channel's envelope so the type id, timestamp and correlation travel with the payload. Publish on a broadcast channel after the state change is durable, from code that holds no receiver references. Consumers subscribe by type, decode the payload, act, and send no reply. Keep the type set closed and versioned, make consumers idempotent and tolerant of unknown types, and define per-type retention (a stale event is often worse than none). The classic object-oriented form - an Event base class with subclasses, a publisher and a subscriber registry - works in-process but serialises across network boundaries. Consider the CNCF CloudEvents v1 format (type, source, id, time, datacontenttype, data) as a vendor-neutral, schema-compatible envelope for cross-system events.
code_sketch:
event OrderPlaced { type: "order.placed.v1", occurred_at: ts, order_id: Id }   # immutable fact
publish(channel: "orders", envelope(headers: {type, occurred_at}, body: OrderPlaced{...}))

# consumer side
subscribe(channel: "orders", type: "order.placed.*"):
    msg = decode(msg.body)                     # payload -> typed event
    apply_idempotently(msg)                    # no reply is sent to the producer
# retention: event.expires_at = published_at + ttl   (a late event is often worse than none)
pitfalls: Treating an event as a command: publishing PlaceOrder and expecting the receiver to act hides an intentional dependency.
Publishing before the state change commits, so consumers observe - and act on - a state that may still roll back.
Thin events that force every consumer to call back to the producer (temporal coupling, extra load) or fat events that copy the whole aggregate on every change.
Assuming exactly-once, ordered delivery; consumers must be idempotent and reorder-tolerant.
Omitting an idempotency key (event id + source) so retry deliveries cause duplicate side-effects.
Failing to dead-letter unprocessable events, letting them vanish silently.
Exposing internal domain model objects as payload, freezing the producer's internal representation as a public contract.

Wrong move: letting a multi-step business process exist only as a chain of event notifications -> no program text shows the flow, so a stuck order surfaces days later and nobody can say which consumer dropped it -> instead make long-lived flows explicit (Process Manager/orchestration), carry correlation ids through every event and instrument publication, consumption lag and dead letters from day one.

Wrong move: consumers inferring behaviour from undocumented aspects of the stream - field presence, ordering, event frequency or the absence of an event -> a producer refactor silently breaks behaviour nobody wrote down -> instead publish explicit per-context event contracts in a schema registry and dead-letter unknown types instead of reading meaning into omissions.

Wrong move: emitting generic filler events like CustomerUpdated because they look reusable -> every consumer reads a different meaning into the same payload, collapsing distinct intents into one ambiguous contract -> instead emit specific past-tense facts (CustomerAddressChanged, EmailVerified) that consumers can subscribe to selectively.
